lessons.title: What RSI Actually Measures
lessons.summary: Explain exactly how RSI is calculated, read any reading as a statement about recent momentum, and stop treating the number as a verdict on price.
lessons.html:
Almost every forex chart you will ever see has an RSI panel underneath it. Ask the trader who put it there what the line measures and the usual answer is "whether the market is overbought or oversold". That answer is incomplete at best, and it is the root of most of the money lost with this indicator.

This course is about one tool, used properly. Before we touch divergence, regimes or entries, we need to know what the number on the screen actually is — because every rule later in the course is built on it. If you understand the arithmetic, you will never again be surprised that RSI "stayed overbought" for two weeks, and you will see divergence for what it really is: a measurement, not a prophecy.

The calculation, without the mystique

The Relative Strength Index was published by J. Welles Wilder in 1978, in the same book that gave us the Average True Range. Wilder was an engineer, and RSI is an engineer's tool: a way of compressing recent momentum into a single number that always sits between 0 and 100.

Here is the whole calculation:

  1. Look at the last 14 candles (14 is Wilder's default and the one this course uses).
  2. For each candle, compare its close with the previous close. If it closed higher, record the gain. If it closed lower, record the loss as a positive number.
  3. Average the gains. Average the losses.
  4. Divide average gain by average loss. That ratio is the "relative strength", RS.
  5. Convert it to a 0–100 scale: RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + RS).

That is the entire indicator. No volume, no sentiment, no order flow. Just the size of recent up-closes compared with the size of recent down-closes.

Three worked numbers make it concrete. Suppose that over the window the average up-close was 12 pips and the average down-close was 4 pips. RS is 3, and RSI is 100 − 100 ÷ 4 = 75. Now suppose up-closes and down-closes averaged 6 pips each. RS is 1, and RSI is exactly 50. Finally, average up-close 4 pips, average down-close 12 pips: RS is a third, RSI is 25.

KEY POINT

RSI answers one question — over the last 14 candles, how large were the up-closes compared with the down-closes?

Speed, not distance

Notice what that question does not ask. It does not ask how far price has travelled. It asks how one-sided the travel was. A market that rises 120 pips in eight clean candles produces almost no down-closes, so average loss is tiny and RSI shoots towards 90. A market that rises the same distance over thirty candles of two-steps-forward, one-step-back produces plenty of down-closes along the way, and RSI might sit in the 60s or low 70s the whole time.

This is the single most important idea in the course. RSI is a speedometer, not a map. It tells you how hard the market has been pushing recently, not where price is. That is why the bounded scale is so useful: an RSI of 75 means the same thing on EUR/USD H1 in 2016 as on gold daily today. You can compare this swing's thrust with the last swing's thrust on the same ruler, which is all divergence trading really is.

What a reading of 50, 70 or 30 actually says

Translate the maths into plain English and the readings become very ordinary:

  • RSI 50 — up-closes and down-closes have been the same size. Momentum is balanced.
  • RSI 70 — recent up-closes have been more than twice the size of recent down-closes (RS is 2.33).
  • RSI 30 — the mirror: down-closes have been more than twice the size of up-closes.

None of those statements says price is "too high", that buyers are exhausted, or that a reversal is due. An RSI of 70 says only that the market has been going up hard relative to how it has been going down. Hold on to that sentence; Lesson 2 is built on it, because "going up hard" is also a perfectly good description of a healthy uptrend.

Wilder's smoothing: RSI has a memory

One wrinkle matters in practice. Wilder did not use a plain 14-bar average. After the first value, each new average is built like this:

new average gain = (previous average gain × 13 + today's gain) ÷ 14

and the same for losses. This behaves like a long exponential average. Each new candle nudges the averages rather than replacing them, so old data fades out gradually instead of dropping off a cliff after 14 bars.

Two consequences follow. First, RSI moves more smoothly than price — one big candle shifts it, but does not reset it. Second, after a violent move, RSI takes time to "forget". A sharp sell-off followed by sideways drift leaves RSI climbing slowly back towards 50 over many candles, even though price is going nowhere. That recovery is the averages decaying, not buyers arriving.

COMMON MISTAKE

reading a slow RSI recovery after a crash as "buyers stepping in". Often it is just the averages decaying. Check the candles before you credit the bulls.

RSI is not a leading indicator

You will hear oscillators sold as "leading" indicators, in contrast to "lagging" moving averages. That is marketing. RSI is calculated entirely from past closes. It cannot contain information about the future, and it turns when price turns, not before.

So what is the honest case for keeping it on your chart? It describes the present more precisely than your eyes can. Momentum fading beneath a rising price is hard to see on candles and easy to see on RSI. Not a crystal ball — a better pair of glasses. Every technique in this course is a way of using those glasses well.

Settings: leave them alone

You can change the lookback. A 7-period RSI is twitchy and visits the extremes constantly. A 21-period RSI is stately and rarely leaves the middle. Shorter settings give more signals of lower quality; longer settings give fewer signals with more lag. There is no magic number.

Our position is simple: stay on 14. Not because 14 is provably optimal — nobody can prove that — but because fiddling with settings is what traders do instead of fixing their process. A divergence that only appears on RSI(9) and vanishes on RSI(14) is a fragile signal. A concept that genuinely works should work on the default.

KEY POINT

the default is a feature. When everyone measures with the same ruler, your observations are repeatable and your testing means something.

Going deeper

Why the scale is bounded. As RS heads towards infinity (no down-closes at all) RSI approaches 100 but never reaches it; as RS approaches zero, RSI approaches 0. The formula compresses the extremes: moving RS from 1 to 2 lifts RSI from 50 to 66.7, but moving it from 4 to 8 only lifts it from 80 to 88.9. Practically, the difference between RSI 85 and 90 represents a much bigger change in the underlying ratio than the difference between 50 and 55. Do not read the scale as linear at the edges.

The seed problem. Wilder's first value is a simple average of the first 14 periods; everything after is smoothed from it. Because the smoothing has a long memory, two platforms that start their calculation from different amounts of history can show slightly different RSI values for the same candle — usually a point or two. That matters if your rules contain sharp thresholds such as "below 40.0". Treat RSI levels as zones (40–50, not 40.0) and you will be immune to it.

Closes only. RSI ignores highs and lows entirely. A long-wicked candle that closes unchanged contributes nothing. That is why a pin bar can reject a level violently while RSI barely moves, and why some divergences look "wrong" if you draw price swings on wicks. We will return to this in Lesson 4: be consistent about whether you draw on closes or wicks.

Timeframe is part of the reading. "RSI is 68" is meaningless without "on which chart". The H1 RSI describes roughly the last day of trading; the daily RSI describes nearly three weeks. In Lesson 9 we give each timeframe a fixed job so the different readings stop arguing with each other.

THE RULES
  • RSI measures the size of recent up-closes relative to recent down-closes — nothing else.
  • Read RSI levels as zones, never as exact thresholds.
  • Use the default 14-period setting unless your own documented testing gives you a reason to change.
  • Always state the timeframe when you quote an RSI reading.

Summary

  • RSI is a smoothed ratio of average up-closes to average down-closes, rescaled to 0–100.
  • It measures the speed and one-sidedness of recent movement, not distance and not "value".
  • 50 means balance; 70 means up-closes have been more than twice the size of down-closes; neither predicts a reversal.
  • Wilder's smoothing gives RSI a memory, so it recovers gradually after violent moves.
  • RSI is not leading. Its edge is describing momentum more precisely than your eyes can.

quiz.q: Over the RSI window, the average up-close is 9 pips and the average down-close is 3 pips. What is the RSI?
Two legs each rise 120 pips. Leg A takes 8 candles with no pullbacks; leg B takes 30 overlapping candles. Which will usually show the higher RSI?
options: Leg B, because it lasted longer
Leg A, because its closes were one-sided
Both the same, because the distance is the same
Impossible to say without volume
quiz.why: RSI compares the size of up-closes with down-closes. Leg A has almost no down-closes, so its ratio — and its RSI — is much higher. Distance alone does not set RSI.

quiz.q: After a sharp sell-off, price goes sideways for twenty candles while RSI rises from 18 to 45. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Strong buying is entering the market
A bullish divergence has formed
The large losses are ageing out of Wilder's smoothed averages
The RSI setting has changed
quiz.why: Wilder's smoothing decays old values gradually. With flat price, the big earlier losses fade and RSI drifts back towards 50 without any meaningful buying.

quiz.q: Which statement about an RSI reading of 72 is correct?
options: Price is too high and should fall
Recent up-closes have been substantially larger than recent down-closes
Buyers are exhausted
A reversal is due within 14 candles
quiz.why: RSI only describes the recent balance of up-closes and down-closes. The other three options are conclusions the maths does not support.

quiz.q: Why does this course recommend keeping the default 14-period setting?
options: 14 is mathematically proven to be optimal
Divergences only exist on 14
A robust concept should work on the default, and changing settings often replaces fixing your process
Shorter settings never give signals
quiz.why: No setting is provably optimal. Staying on the default keeps observations repeatable and stops you curve-fitting settings to past charts.

lessons.title: The Overbought and Oversold Myth
lessons.summary: Recognise why "sell above 70, buy below 30" fails in trends, identify the one regime where it can work, and replace the myth with a context-first rule.
lessons.html:
Every trading platform ships RSI with two dotted lines, at 70 and 30. Every beginner guide repeats the same instruction: above 70 the market is overbought, so sell; below 30 it is oversold, so buy. It sounds sensible. It feels contrarian and clever. And in a trending market — which is exactly when RSI spends the most time beyond those lines — it is a reliable way of losing money slowly.

This lesson takes the myth apart using nothing but what you learned in Lesson 1, then rebuilds the small piece of it that is genuinely useful.

What "overbought" really looks like

Recall the arithmetic. RSI above 70 means recent up-closes have been more than twice the size of recent down-closes. Now ask the question the folklore skips: what kind of market produces that?

A strong uptrend. When a pair is trending hard it closes up more often than down, and the up-closes are bigger. RSI does not merely visit 70 in those conditions — it moves in and unpacks. Analysts call this an embedded reading: RSI holding above 70 (or below 30) for bar after bar. An embedded reading is not a reversal warning. It is the market saying, in the plainest language an indicator can manage, that the trend is powerful and one-sided.

The trader who shorts every touch of 70 is systematically fading strength. In a quiet range they will feel clever. Then a real trend arrives, RSI pins above 70 for a fortnight, and they experience the special pain of being repeatedly and confidently wrong in the same direction.

"Overbought" was always a strange word. It smuggles in a conclusion — that too much buying has happened and must be corrected — that the maths does not support. RSI at 74 is a thermometer reading. Deciding the patient must therefore cool down imminently is your assumption, not the thermometer's.

KEY POINT

RSI above 70 is the signature of strength first. It only becomes a reason to sell when something else — the regime and the structure — says so.

The mirror image costs just as much

Oversold buying in a downtrend is the same mistake upside down, and it usually hurts more, because falling markets tend to move faster than rising ones.

Notice where that losing trade went wrong. Not in the stop placement and not in the size: the stop did its job and capped the loss at one R. The error was the premise. The trader read a description of strong selling as a prediction that selling would stop.

Where the folklore does hold

We promised honest, not one-eyed. Overbought and oversold logic is not useless — it is conditional, and the condition is the market regime.

In a genuine range — price oscillating between clear support and resistance with no trend — mean reversion is the dominant behaviour. Each leg runs into the opposite boundary and turns. RSI extremes then tend to coincide with the edges of the range, and fading them towards the middle or the other side is a coherent idea worth testing.

Look closely at that trade. The reason to sell was the level — a ceiling that had already turned price twice. RSI near 70 added a second, independent piece of evidence: the push into the ceiling was stretched. Take away the level and RSI 72 on its own would have told you nothing.

Ranges end — and the last fade loses

Ranges do not last forever, and they usually end with a breakout that RSI reads as maximally overbought (or oversold) at precisely the wrong moment. The range trader's nightmare arrives on schedule: the market pushes through the ceiling, RSI prints 72, and the habit says "fade it".

Two honest lessons sit in that chart. First, any range-fading rule needs a stop beyond the range and an acceptance that some fades will lose — that is a cost of doing business, not a failure. Second, mid-range RSI readings are noise. RSI at 65 while price floats in the middle of a range tells you nothing worth risking money on. Extremes matter at the edges, where structure gives them something to lean on.

COMMON MISTAKE

"regime denial" — fading a breakout because the range has paid for three weeks. The market does not consult your comfort before changing character. Lesson 3 gives you a checklist that overrules your preferences.

Why the myth is so sticky

If fading extremes loses so reliably in trends, why does everyone keep doing it? Because fading feels intelligent. Buying a market that is already up smells like arriving late; selling it feels like seeing through the crowd. Calling a top is ego food. Trend-following, by contrast, feels like queueing.

Loss aversion makes it worse. A fade that works pays quickly, which is intoxicating. A fade that fails loses slowly and invites averaging in — "it's even more overbought now" — which is how a small wrong idea becomes a large wrong position.

The replacement rule

Here is the rule this course uses instead, and it inverts the folklore:

  1. In a trend, treat RSI extremes as evidence of strength. RSI above 70 in an uptrend is a reason to respect the trend and look for pullback entries in its direction, not tops.
  2. In a confirmed range, an extreme at the boundary is a candidate fade. Only at the boundary, only with structure agreeing, and only with a stop beyond the range.
  3. Anywhere, an extreme is a reason not to chase. If RSI has just spiked to 85 on a vertical candle, your entry would sit at the far end of a stretched move, your stop would be a long way off, and any ordinary pullback would hurt. Do not fade it, but do not chase it either.

Same number, opposite meanings — and the difference is entirely context. The indicator cannot know the context. You can.

A thirty-second test before any fade

Whenever you feel the pull to sell a high reading or buy a low one, run three questions before you touch the order ticket:

  1. Is there a range? Can you point to at least two clean touches of both a ceiling and a floor, with swings overlapping between them? If you cannot, there is no range — there is a trend or a mess, and neither is a place to fade.
  2. Is price at the boundary? Not near it, not "heading towards" it — at it. A fade from the middle of the box has no structural reason to work and nowhere sensible for a stop.
  3. Where is the stop, and does the trade still pay? The stop belongs beyond the boundary, not at an arbitrary distance. Measure from entry to that stop, then to the far side of the range. If the reward is less than twice the risk, the trade fails on arithmetic before RSI enters the conversation.

Notice that RSI only appears after the third question. That is deliberate. In a range the reading is a supporting witness, not the prosecution's whole case. Most of the time this test will tell you to do nothing, which is precisely what it is for.

Going deeper

Why extremes cluster in trends. With Wilder's 14-period smoothing, RSI only reaches 70 when RS exceeds 2.33. A trend that closes up on two candles out of three, with up-closes about as large as down-closes, already gets you there. So trending markets mechanically generate extremes; they are the base case, not the exception. Fading every extreme means fading the base case.

Extremes as a stretch measure. There is a softer, legitimate use of a high reading inside a trend: as a measure of how extended the latest leg is. If your pullback strategy needs room to a target, a reading of 85 at the moment you would enter tells you the leg is already mature and the next pullback is likely to be deeper than average. That is useful for management — waiting for the pullback, setting realistic targets — not for counter-trend entries.

Some extremes do mark tops. Sometimes RSI hits 78 and the market reverses that hour. The point is not that fading always fails; it is that "70 means sell" contains no edge by itself, because it fires constantly in exactly the conditions where it is most wrong. Whatever edge exists lives in the filter — regime, level, structure — not in the number. Lessons 3 and 7 build those filters.

Hypothetical expectancy check. Suppose, purely for illustration, a fade-every-extreme rule wins 55% of trades in ranges at +1R, but in trends the same rule wins 35% at +1R and loses 1R otherwise. If a third of your sample is trending, the blended result is roughly (2/3 × 0.10) + (1/3 × −0.30) ≈ −0.03R per trade. A small regime filter that removed the trend trades would turn that into +0.10R. The numbers are invented; the shape of the argument is not.

THE RULES
  • Never sell solely because RSI is above 70, or buy solely because it is below 30.
  • In a diagnosed trend, extremes confirm the trend; look for entries in its direction.
  • Fade an extreme only at the boundary of a confirmed range, with the stop beyond the range.
  • Ignore RSI extremes that form in the middle of a range or in the middle of nowhere.

Summary

  • RSI above 70 means up-closes have dominated — the definition of a strong uptrend, not a top.
  • Embedded readings (RSI holding beyond 70 or 30) are a trend signature; fading them is fading strength.
  • In a genuine range, extremes at the boundaries can support a fade, with a stop beyond the range.
  • Ranges end with breakouts that look maximally "overbought"; the last fade loses and the stop must absorb it.
  • Replace the myth with context: strength in trends, boundary fades in ranges, no chasing anywhere.

quiz.q: EUR/USD has made three higher highs on the H4 and RSI has been between 72 and 88 for 40 candles. What does the RSI reading most likely describe?
options: A market about to reverse
A strong, one-sided uptrend
A range about to break down
A bearish divergence
quiz.why: An embedded reading above 70 is what a powerful trend looks like mathematically: up-closes dominating for a long time. It is not a reversal signal.

quiz.q: In which situation is fading an RSI extreme a coherent idea to test?
options: RSI at 75 in the middle of a strong uptrend
RSI at 28 in a downtrend making lower lows
RSI at 73 as price tests the ceiling of a well-defined range
RSI at 65 in the middle of a range
quiz.why: Only at the boundary of a confirmed range does an extreme coincide with a level where reversal is the ordinary outcome. The others are trend signatures or mid-range noise.

quiz.q: A range has paid you three times at its ceiling. Price now closes above the ceiling with RSI at 72. Which response matches this lesson?
options: Sell, because RSI is overbought and the range has worked
Add to the short with a wider stop
Treat it as a possible regime change; if you do fade, your stop beyond structure must be honoured
Buy immediately because breakouts always continue
quiz.why: Ranges end with breakouts that look overbought. Regime denial is the trap. A breakout is evidence the regime may have changed, and any fade must be capped by its stop.

quiz.q: RSI spikes to 86 on a single vertical candle in an uptrend. What is the grown-up reading?
options: Sell immediately
Buy immediately before it goes higher
Don't fade it, but don't chase it — wait for a pullback
Switch to a 21-period RSI
quiz.why: An extreme in a trend is strength, so fading is wrong; but entering at the far end of a stretched leg gives poor stop placement and poor reward, so chasing is wrong too.

quiz.q: In the 'Buying oversold in a downtrend' chart, what was the real error in the losing trade?
options: The stop was too tight
The position was too large
The premise: it treated a description of strong selling as a prediction that selling would stop
The target was too far away
quiz.why: The stop capped the loss at one R as designed. The trade should never have been taken, because 'oversold' in a downtrend describes the trend rather than ending it.

lessons.title: RSI Regimes — The 40–80 and 20–60 Ranges
lessons.summary: Diagnose whether a market is trending up, trending down or ranging from structure and RSI's own behaviour, and read every RSI value in the light of that regime.
lessons.html:
Lesson 2 tore down the overbought/oversold folklore. This lesson builds the replacement: a working model of how RSI behaves in the two regimes that matter — trends and ranges. Learn it and the indicator stops being two arbitrary dotted lines and becomes a regime gauge, which is arguably its most underrated job.

The core observation is simple, and once you have seen it you cannot unsee it: RSI does not use its 0–100 scale evenly. In a trend, its working range shifts.

The bull range: 40 to 80

In a healthy uptrend, RSI typically oscillates between roughly 40 and 80. Rallies push it into the 70s or low 80s. Pullbacks drain it back to the 40s or low 50s, and then it turns up again. The 30 line is rarely touched, because even the sell-offs in an uptrend lack the sustained down-closes needed to drag the ratio that low.

Traders sometimes call the 40–50 area in an uptrend the bull support zone for RSI: it is where pullbacks tend to run out of downside momentum. This idea was explored in depth by Andrew Cardwell and later popularised by Constance Brown, and it is one of the few pieces of indicator lore that survives contact with real charts. Do not take it on trust — mark RSI's swing highs and lows through any sustained trend on a major pair and see where they cluster.

KEY POINT

in an uptrend, "RSI back to 40–50" means the pullback is mature. It is a place to start looking for longs, not a sign of weakness.

The bear range: 20 to 60

In a downtrend, mirror everything. RSI lives roughly between 20 and 60. Bounces stall in the 50s or low 60s; declines press into the 20s. The 70 line might as well not be on the chart.

In the bear range, the 50–60 area is the bear resistance zone: where rallies tend to run out of upside momentum. A bounce that reaches it and rolls over is the downtrend doing what downtrends do.

Ranges: the full span

In a genuine sideways market, RSI uses more of its scale: it swings from the 30s to the 70s, with the extremes roughly matching the edges of the range. You saw this in Lesson 2. It is the one regime where the platform's default 70/30 lines are roughly the right landmarks — and even there, only at the boundaries.

So you have three signatures:

Regime Typical RSI working range Where pullbacks/bounces end
Uptrend about 40–80 40–50 (bull support zone)
Downtrend about 20–60 50–60 (bear resistance zone)
Range about 30–70 extremes near the range edges

Treat these as zones, not laws. A strong trend may run 45–85; a gentle one 40–70. What matters is the shift: which half of the scale RSI is living in.

When the regime breaks

The practical payoff is not just recognising pullbacks. It is noticing when something has changed. In an uptrend, RSI dropping through 40 and reaching 30 is a move that was structurally "impossible" in the old regime. It is the momentum equivalent of a lower low.

That does not automatically make a downtrend. A single dip to 30 can be a violent pullback in a trend that recovers. But it is a fact that the old regime did not produce, and it should sharpen your attention. If the next bounce stalls with RSI in the 50s — the bear resistance zone — and price prints a lower high, structure and momentum are now telling the same new story.

COMMON MISTAKE

treating an RSI regime shift as a sell signal on its own. It is a change in the background, not a trigger. You still need a level and a confirmation (Lessons 7 and 8).

Diagnosing the regime in thirty seconds

Everything above is useless if you cannot tell which regime you are in, so make the diagnosis explicit. Three checks, ten seconds each, in this order:

  1. Structure. Is price printing higher highs and higher lows, lower highs and lower lows, or overlapping swings between horizontal levels? Structure is the primary evidence. Price first, indicator second.
  2. RSI's own recent range. Over the last 40–60 candles, where have RSI's swing lows and highs clustered? 40–80 suggests up; 20–60 suggests down; full-span turns at both ends suggests a range. The indicator diagnoses itself.
  3. The 50 line. Momentum that consistently holds above 50 leans bullish; consistently below leans bearish; endless whipsawing across 50 is the signature of chop.

If all three agree, you have a regime. If they disagree — structure says up but RSI has started living in 30–60 — you have a market in transition, and the honest answer is usually "no new trades until it settles".

Regime first, reading second

The discipline is doing the diagnosis before consulting the signal. Most RSI disasters are not caused by the indicator misfiring. They are caused by a range tactic being deployed in a trend, or a trend tactic in a range. Same panel, same settings, same trader — wrong map.

A worked diagnosis

Here is the thirty-second routine applied to an illustrative chart, so you can see what the written output looks like. EUR/USD, H4, last 60 candles.

Structure. Swing highs at 1.0890, 1.0935 and 1.0982; swing lows at 1.0841, 1.0878 and 1.0921. Each high is higher than the last, each low is higher than the last. Verdict: uptrend.

RSI's own range. RSI swing lows at the three pullbacks read 47, 44 and 51. RSI swing highs read 78, 74 and 81. The working range is roughly 44–81. Verdict: bull regime.

The 50 line. RSI has closed below 50 on only four of the last 60 candles, each time briefly. Verdict: bullish.

The sentence: "EUR/USD H4 is in an uptrend; I am interested only in longs, ideally from pullbacks that reset RSI to the 40–50 area."

That sentence does an enormous amount of work. It rules out every short. It rules out buying stretched rallies with RSI at 80. It tells you what a good opportunity will look like before it arrives, so that when RSI next drops to 46 at a higher low you recognise it rather than fear it. And it gives you a clear condition for changing your mind: a lower low in price, or an RSI swing low below about 38, would send you back to the checklist.

Run the routine at the start of each session and write the sentence down. It takes less time than reading one news headline.

There is a psychological trap worth naming here: regime denial. Traders who have been profitably fading a range for three weeks do not want the range to end, so they treat the breakout as just another extreme. Write your regime criteria down, check them at the start of every session, and let the checklist overrule your preferences.

Going deeper

Why the range shifts. It falls straight out of the arithmetic. In an uptrend, pullbacks are typically shorter and shallower than rallies. Wilder's smoothed average gain stays elevated through a brief pullback, so RS rarely falls below about 0.67 — which is RSI 40. Only a pullback that is both deep and sustained can push RS below 0.43 (RSI 30). That is why RSI 30 in an uptrend is evidence the character of the down-moves has changed.

Range "failures" as information. Cardwell's framing is useful: in an uptrend, the important event is not RSI reaching 70 but RSI failing to fall below 40. In a downtrend, it is RSI failing to rise above 60. When a regime's floor or ceiling breaks, you have the momentum equivalent of a broken swing. Combined with a broken swing in price, it is a strong regime-change case.

Timeframe matters. The regime on the H1 can be a downtrend while the daily is a clean uptrend — the H1 "downtrend" is simply the daily pullback. Lesson 9 assigns the regime job to the higher timeframe so these readings stop competing.

Thresholds are fuzzy by design. A disciplined trader might write "uptrend if the last three RSI swing lows were all above 38 and price structure shows HH/HL". That is testable. "RSI looks bullish" is not. Write your version down; Lesson 10 includes a template.

THE RULES
  • Diagnose the regime before reading any RSI value: structure first, RSI range second, 50 line third.
  • In an uptrend, RSI pullbacks to 40–50 mark mature pullbacks, not weakness.
  • In a downtrend, RSI bounces to 50–60 mark mature bounces, not strength.
  • If structure and RSI regime disagree, treat the market as in transition and stand aside.

Summary

  • RSI's working range shifts with the trend: about 40–80 in uptrends, 20–60 in downtrends, 30–70 in ranges.
  • The 40–50 bull support zone and 50–60 bear resistance zone mark where pullbacks typically exhaust.
  • An uptrend RSI reaching 30, or a downtrend RSI reaching 70, is the momentum version of a broken swing.
  • Diagnose regime with structure, RSI's own range and the 50 line — before reading any signal.
  • Disagreement between the checks means transition: the default answer is no trade.

lessons.title: Regular Divergence — Momentum Fading at the Extremes
lessons.summary: Identify and draw regular bullish and bearish divergence correctly between genuine swings, explain why it forms, and treat it as an early warning rather than an entry.
lessons.html:
This is the headline act, and the reason most serious traders keep RSI on their charts long after abandoning the 70/30 folklore. Regular divergence is the moment when price and momentum stop telling the same story: price pushes to a new extreme, but the force behind the push is weaker than last time.

Used well, it is one of the most informative things an oscillator can show you. Used badly — and it is usually used badly — it is a machine for shorting strong uptrends with a clear conscience. This lesson teaches you to see it, draw it honestly, and respect its limits.

The two patterns

Regular bearish divergence: price makes a higher high, but RSI makes a lower high.

Regular bullish divergence: price makes a lower low, but RSI makes a higher low.

In both cases price has extended the move, but the momentum behind the extension has faded. The engine is still turning; it is turning with less force than before.

Why divergence happens

Remember what RSI measures: the size of recent up-closes relative to recent down-closes. Late in a move, the final push to a new extreme is often ground out — smaller candles, more overlap, hesitant closes — compared with the muscular impulse that built the earlier high. Price nudges over the line; the average gain does not keep up. So RSI prints a lower high even as price prints a higher one.

Divergence is not magic. It is arithmetic noticing what your eye glosses over: the new extreme was achieved with less conviction.

The bullish version is identical logic upside down. A downtrend stabs to a lower low, but the selling behind that stab is weaker than at the previous low, so RSI holds a higher low. Sellers are still winning — but on fumes.

KEY POINT

regular divergence means the new extreme was reached with less momentum. It describes fading force — it does not say the move is over.

A worked illustration in the candles

Here is the same idea with the candles doing the talking (an illustration of technique, not a signal). GBP/USD on the H4 rallies from about 1.2600 to 1.2855 in a burst of a few large, clean candles. It pauses and pulls back, then pushes to around 1.2874. But look at how it gets there: the second push takes many more candles, with smaller bodies and plenty of overlap.

RSI peaked in the mid-90s on the first high and only in the high 60s on the second. That is a complete regular bearish divergence: a marginal new price high, a decisively lower momentum high, and fading conviction visible in both the candles and the maths.

What does a disciplined trader do with it? Nothing, yet. They mark it. They stop looking for new longs. They wait for structure to speak — which is the subject of Lessons 7 and 8.

Warning, not signal

This is the part most RSI content rushes past, and the part that decides whether divergence makes or costs you money. Regular divergence is an early warning, not an entry.

"Early" is doing heavy lifting in that sentence. Momentum can fade for a long time before price turns. Strong trends routinely print one divergence after another, each looking like the top. And sometimes momentum resets through time: price goes sideways for twenty candles, RSI drifts back to the middle, and the trend simply resumes.

So calibrate your expectations now. Divergence marks conditions, not timing. It says: "the move is ageing; stop adding in this direction; start paying attention to the other side." It does not say "reverse here".

COMMON MISTAKE

shorting the first bearish divergence in a strong uptrend. That is the Lesson 2 mistake — fading strength — with extra homework.

Drawing it properly

Divergence sounds simple and is easy to draw wrong. These craft rules protect you from the most common self-deceptions.

Compare swings, not wiggles. A divergence connects two meaningful swing highs (or lows) in price with the RSI values at those same candles. A useful mechanical test: each point should be the highest high (or lowest low) of at least three candles either side. If you cannot identify the two price swings on a naked chart first, the divergence does not exist.

Match the peaks in time. The RSI value you use must be the one produced by that price swing, not a convenient peak from somewhere nearby. Draw a vertical line if you have to. Cherry-picking oscillator points to manufacture a slope is the most popular form of divergence fraud, and the only victim is you.

Use adjacent swings. Compare the latest swing with the one immediately before it. Skipping over an intermediate swing to find a pair that diverges is another way of seeing what you want to see.

Prefer divergence at extremes. A bearish divergence whose first RSI peak sat above 70 carries more information than one where both peaks idled around 55. Fading momentum at a genuine extreme is the pattern with pedigree; mid-range wobbles are common and mostly meaningless.

Be consistent about closes and wicks. RSI is built from closes, so momentum peaks align with closing prices. Whether you mark price swings on wicks or closes matters less than doing it the same way every time.

A drawing routine you can repeat

Here is the routine, in order, that turns those craft rules into something mechanical. Use it every time, especially when you are excited about what you think you see.

  1. Cover the RSI panel. On the naked chart, mark the last two swing highs (for bearish) or swing lows (for bullish) using your fractal rule — the highest high or lowest low of at least three candles either side.
  2. Compare the prices. For regular bearish divergence the second high must be higher than the first; for regular bullish, the second low must be lower. If price did not make a new extreme, stop: whatever you see on RSI, it is not regular divergence.
  3. Uncover RSI and read it at those exact candles. Not at a nearby peak, not at the highest point in the area — at the candles you marked.
  4. Measure the gap. Second reading lower than the first (bearish) or higher (bullish) by at least 4–5 points? If not, there is no meaningful divergence.
  5. Note where the first reading was. Above 70 (bearish) or below 30 (bullish) adds weight. Both readings parked in the 50s adds very little.
  6. Write it down — pair, timeframe, the two prices, the two RSI values. If you cannot fill in all six numbers, you have a feeling, not a divergence.

Run this on the training charts in this lesson and you will find every one passes. Run it on your own charts and you will find that a surprising share of the divergences you thought you saw do not. That is not a failure of the routine; it is the routine doing its job. The single most common drawing error in practice is skipping step 1 — looking at RSI first, finding a slope, and then hunting for price swings to match it.

Going deeper

Magnitude matters, within limits. A divergence where RSI drops from 85 to 62 says more than one where it drops from 72 to 70. A two-point difference is within the noise of different platforms' calculations (Lesson 1's seed problem). As a working rule, ignore RSI differences of less than about 4–5 points.

Distance between swings. Divergences between swings 10–40 candles apart on your chosen timeframe tend to be meaningful. Swings three candles apart are one move; swings 120 candles apart belong to different market phases and the comparison loses meaning.

The scale compresses at extremes. Because the RSI formula squashes high RS values (Lesson 1), a drop from 90 to 80 represents a larger fall in the underlying gain/loss ratio than a drop from 60 to 50. Divergence from very high readings is therefore more pronounced in the underlying maths than it looks.

Divergence and regime. In a strong uptrend whose RSI lives at 45–90, a bearish divergence from 88 to 74 leaves RSI still in the bull range. That is momentum cooling, not momentum breaking. Compare it with a divergence whose second peak fails below 60 — beneath the bull range — which is a far more serious statement. Lesson 3's regime ranges give you the context to grade it.

THE RULES
  • Regular bearish divergence: price higher high, RSI lower high. Regular bullish: price lower low, RSI higher low.
  • Draw divergence only between two adjacent, genuine swing points, with RSI read at those same candles.
  • Ignore RSI differences smaller than about 4–5 points.
  • Regular divergence is a warning: stop adding in the trend's direction, but never enter on the divergence alone.

Summary

  • Regular divergence shows a new price extreme reached with weaker momentum.
  • It forms because late pushes are often ground out with overlapping candles, so average gains (or losses) shrink.
  • Draw it between adjacent, genuine swings, with RSI read at the same candles, and prefer divergences that start from an extreme.
  • It is an early warning of fading momentum, not a reversal signal; trends often continue or go sideways.
  • The action it justifies on its own is limited: stop adding, mark it, and wait for structure.

Too small to count — within the noise

Bullish divergence

Double your long position

RSI is broken on gold

lessons.title: Hidden Divergence — The Trend-Continuation Clue
lessons.summary: Identify hidden bullish and bearish divergence inside an established trend, explain why it signals continuation, and know exactly where the idea is invalidated.
lessons.html:
If regular divergence is the famous sibling, hidden divergence is the quietly competent one who gets more done. It points with the trend rather than against it, so it co-operates with the market's default behaviour instead of fighting it. For most intermediate traders it is the more forgiving pattern to trade — and it is the one that gets confused with regular divergence more than any other.

This lesson gives you the definitions, the mechanics, and the two conditions without which hidden divergence is just noise in a costume.

The pattern, flipped

Hidden bullish divergence: price makes a higher low, but RSI makes a lower low.

Hidden bearish divergence: price makes a lower high, but RSI makes a higher high.

Read those twice, because they are regular divergence's mirror image. A crude but reliable memory aid:

  • Regular divergence disagrees at the extremes of the move — new price extreme, weaker momentum — and warns of a possible reversal.
  • Hidden divergence disagrees at the pullbacks — protected price level, deeper momentum reset — and suggests continuation.

Another way to remember it: for bullish setups, regular divergence is read on lows that go down in price; hidden divergence is read on lows that go up in price. In both bullish cases you compare lows; in both bearish cases you compare highs.

Why it means continuation

Walk through the bullish case slowly. An uptrend pulls back. The pullback holds above the previous swing low — a higher low, so the trend is technically healthy. But this pullback was sharp: several heavy sell candles compressed into a short time. RSI, which measures the size of recent down-closes, reads that sharpness as a deep momentum flush and prints a lower low than it did at the previous, gentler pullback.

So price says "the trend is fine — buyers defended a higher floor", while RSI says "that dip was violent".

Why is that bullish? Because the market absorbed an outsized dose of selling and still could not break structure. Momentum has been fully reset — the spring recompressed — without the trend conceding anything. When the sellers' best recent effort produces only a higher low, the path of least resistance remains up.

The bearish mirror works the same way. A downtrend bounces; the bounce is punchy enough to push RSI to a higher high than the previous rally managed, but price stalls at a lower high. Buyers threw real momentum at it and still could not reclaim structure.

KEY POINT

hidden divergence is a momentum reset inside an intact trend. It nominates a pullback as finished; it does not create a trend where there isn't one.

Why with-trend divergence is the friendlier tool

Regular divergence asks you to bet that a trend is ending — an event that is relatively rare and hard to time. Hidden divergence asks you to bet that a trend will continue — the more ordinary outcome — and merely helps you time the entry. One fights the base rate; the other rides it.

There is a second advantage, and in practice it matters more: crisp invalidation. The whole idea is "the pullback ended at a protected higher low". If price breaks that low, the pattern is dead and the trend itself is in question. Your stop has an obvious home just beyond it. With regular divergence, invalidation is fuzzier, because trends can print a new extreme and still reverse shortly after.

A complete example — and its failure

Here is the pattern taken as a trade, with an illustrative risk of 1% of the account (technique, not a signal). EUR/USD H1 is in a diagnosed uptrend. The second pullback is sharp, holds a higher low, and RSI prints a lower low. The pullback ends with a bullish engulfing candle — the trigger (Lesson 8 covers triggers in detail).

Now the version every honest course must show. Same trend, same pattern, same trigger, same stop logic. This time the higher low does not hold.

Study that losing trade, because it is what a correct loss looks like. The stop sat where the idea became false, the loss was capped at the planned 1R, and the market then showed — through a break of structure and an RSI regime break — that the trend had genuinely changed. You cannot avoid trades like this. You can make sure each one costs exactly what you planned.

COMMON MISTAKE

moving the stop below the next, lower swing "to give it room". Once the higher low breaks, the hidden divergence no longer exists. Extra room only buys a larger loss on a dead idea.

The craft rules

Everything from Lesson 4 carries over — real swings, adjacent swings, RSI read at the same candles, no cherry-picking — plus three rules specific to hidden divergence:

  1. The trend must exist. Hidden divergence is a continuation pattern; without an established trend there is nothing to continue. Run Lesson 3's diagnosis first: higher highs and higher lows, RSI living in its bull range. Hidden divergence "found" inside a choppy range is noise.
  2. Where RSI resets matters. The best hidden bullish divergences see RSI dip into the 40–50 bull support zone — a full reset within a healthy regime. If RSI collapses to 25 in your "uptrend", question the uptrend, not just the entry.
  3. Where in the trend matters. A hidden divergence at the second or third pullback of a young trend is a different proposition from one at the eighth pullback of an old, extended move. The pattern does not know how old the trend is. You should.

Hidden divergence or just a pullback?

Most pullbacks in a trend are not hidden divergence, and that is fine. The label only applies when all four of these are true:

  • Two pullbacks to compare. You need an earlier swing low (for bullish) and a later one, both genuine fractal swings in the same trend.
  • Price protected the level. The later swing low is clearly above the earlier one. "About the same" is not a higher low; a double bottom is a different pattern with a different story.
  • RSI went deeper. The RSI value at the later low is at least 4–5 points below the RSI value at the earlier low.
  • The trend is real. Lesson 3's diagnosis said uptrend before you looked for the pattern, not after.

A short worked illustration (technique, not a signal): GBP/USD H4 in a diagnosed uptrend. The first pullback drifts over nine candles to 1.2710, with RSI bottoming at 52. The rally reaches 1.2830. The second pullback drops in four heavy candles to 1.2745 — 35 pips above the first low — and RSI bottoms at 43. All four conditions pass: two genuine swing lows, a protected higher low, RSI 9 points deeper, a trend already diagnosed. That is a candidate, waiting only for a level check and a trigger.

Change one fact — say the second pullback had dropped to 1.2712, two pips above the first — and the honest description becomes "a test of the prior low". It may still bounce, but it is no longer a clearly protected higher low, and the crisp invalidation that makes hidden divergence attractive has gone.

Going deeper

Hidden divergence and pullback speed. The mechanism depends on the second pullback being faster than the first. A slow, deep pullback that holds a higher low can still leave RSI higher than at the first low, because the down-closes are small and spread out. That is not hidden divergence — but it is not necessarily bad either. It is just a pullback. Do not force the label.

The overlap with regular divergence on a lower timeframe. A sharp pullback in a higher-timeframe uptrend is a small downtrend on the lower timeframe. As it exhausts into support, that lower timeframe often prints regular bullish divergence. So a single event can appear as hidden divergence on the H4 and regular divergence on the M15. Lesson 9 uses this deliberately.

Distance from the trend's mean. Hidden divergence where the higher low also sits near a rising 50 EMA or a prior breakout level has a second, independent reason to hold. Lesson 7 makes location a hard requirement.

Hypothetical expectancy. Suppose — purely for illustration — that with-trend hidden divergence setups win 45% of the time at an average of +2.2R, and lose 1R otherwise. Expectancy would be 0.45 × 2.2 − 0.55 × 1 ≈ +0.44R per trade. The point is not the invented numbers; it is that a pattern can lose more often than it wins and still be worth trading if the geometry is right. Lesson 9 and your own testing do the real work.

THE RULES
  • Hidden bullish: price higher low, RSI lower low. Hidden bearish: price lower high, RSI higher high.
  • Only look for hidden divergence inside a diagnosed trend, in the trend's direction.
  • Prefer hidden bullish divergence where RSI resets to roughly 40–50 (or 50–60 for bearish).
  • The protected swing is the invalidation: if it breaks, the setup is dead and the stop is taken without adjustment.

Summary

  • Hidden divergence compares the pullbacks: higher low with lower RSI low (bullish), lower high with higher RSI high (bearish).
  • It shows a full momentum reset that failed to break structure — a continuation clue.
  • It trades with the base rate and has crisp invalidation at the protected swing.
  • It needs an established trend; in a range it means nothing.
  • Correct losses happen: when the protected swing breaks, accept the planned 1R and move on.

Hidden bearish divergence

A bearish candle after entry

Trade it with double size

The trader closed early at breakeven
The target was reached later
quiz.why: A correct loss is one where the stop enforces the invalidation and the loss equals the risk planned before entry.
